attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, in his own voice, answering a booster quip.

semantics.note: 'Nobody will do it' is a firm forecast with no hedge and no deadline. The normalised wording keeps the AI 2027 self-learning agent as the target. The past-tense parts ('no proof', 'nobody has done it') are rightly left out of the score.

contract.note: Reading the claim against AI 2027's agent that keeps learning to do research and engineering is the ordinary contextual reading. It is right that narrow self-modification does not count automatically, and that the title 'AI 2027' is not treated as a deadline. Fair, but the result depends on that reading.

evidence.note: The AI 2027 scenario text. It defines the premise being criticised but is fiction, not an observed outcome.

The Darwin Gödel Machine preprint: an agent that rewrites its own code and improves on coding benchmarks. It is narrower than the AI 2027 capability and has no independent evaluation, so it does not meet the contradiction condition.
An October 2026 preprint finding that current self-evolving agents are incomplete continual learners. This limits what exists today but proves nothing about whether it is impossible later.

reviews.rationale: This is a firm forecast with no deadline. Nothing in the packet shows an independently evaluated agent that meets the contradiction condition: the Darwin Gödel Machine is narrower and was not independently evaluated. Nothing proves impossibility either. Not seeing a qualifying agent in a finite period cannot support a 'never' forecast, so the claim stays open and unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words, given as his conclusion after discussing the MIT study.

semantics.note: 'Isn't...going to save' is a firm forecast with no deadline. The 'because' clause is a stated reason, not a condition, and is kept as such. The word 'suddenly' is dropped, which matters little.

contract.note: Reading 'save' as enterprise sales making the leading AI providers financially self-sustaining is an ordinary reading of the post. It neither stretches the claim for nor against him. The speaker named no companies and no measure, so the reading decides the result.

evidence.note: Anthropic's S-1 filing: a net loss for H1 2026, mostly from fair-value changes on convertible notes, alongside about $3.9B of positive operating cash flow. It does not separate out enterprise funding or show durable self-sufficiency, and it shows no business failure.

reviews.rationale: No deadline was given. The only evidence is Anthropic's filing: net losses, but positive operating cash flow over six months. That falls short of durable self-sufficiency funded by enterprise customers, and no major provider has failed. Neither the early-resolution condition nor the contradiction condition is met, so the forecast stays open.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: 'Are not going to go bust' is firm. The normalised claim keeps both the 'once the AI bubble bursts' condition and the 'for the most part' scope, and correctly leaves out the 42% NVIDIA figure.

contract.note: Reading the target as the major tech companies buying GPUs, and 'go bust' as bankruptcy or similar failure, is ordinary. Counting 'for the most part' by number of companies is a reasonable choice, and the contract flags that ambiguity. Requiring a broad collapse rather than a regional one is fair.

evidence.note: An IMF blog from October 2026 that treats an AI correction as a risk scenario. It does not show that a collapse has happened.
A Reuters report of a crash in Chinese AI stocks, with only a 6% Nasdaq drawdown in the US. A regional burst does not establish the broad collapse affecting the major buyers.

reviews.rationale: The forecast depends on the AI bubble bursting, and the packet does not show that it has: the crash is regional, in China, and the US decline is minor. Because that condition is not met, the forecast cannot be scored. The packet also has no record of buyer insolvencies.

attribution.note: Zitron's own calculation, set out in his own post.

semantics.note: This is an estimate built on the speaker's stated 30% assumption. The normalised claim keeps that assumption and the 'from 2024' scope.

contract.note: Grading the calculation he disclosed, rather than an accounting loss, is fair. It also fairly treats 30% as his assumption and allows ordinary rounding. Whether the credit facility counts as funding, and how capex is defined, decide the result.

evidence.note: A Crunchbase-based estimate of $18.2B cumulative funding as of March 2025. It does not cover funding through August 2025.
The $2.5B is a revolving credit facility. It is not shown to have been drawn, so counting it as funding received is unverified.
The ~$105B is a 2025 plan under Amazon's net, lease-inclusive definition, which differs from gross purchases. The packet does not directly verify the $83B 2024 input.
The speaker's own post. It shows how the arithmetic is reconstructed, but his statement cannot prove itself.

reviews.rationale: The arithmetic reproduces $77.1B from the inputs as reported. But the inputs are not verified on a consistent basis. Funding is only established up to March 2025, the credit facility is not shown to have been drawn, and the capex inputs mix definitions, with the $83B 2024 figure never confirmed. Dropping the credit line would change the total only slightly, but the packet does not settle the total either way.
